solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

parts.note: your go is your turn in a game

indicators.note: something returned is sent back the way it came, so its letters run backwards

parts.note: to do someone is British slang for cheating them

explanation.surface: A kind person turns on someone who cheated them and gets their own back.
explanation.walkthrough: "Kind" looks like a noun (a sort), but it is the adjective: good-hearted.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a kind deed and a good deed are the same thing, both meaning benevolent.

indicators.note: breaking something smashes it apart, so the letters are broken up and put back together differently

explanation.surface: A spy-thriller plot: a star secret agent breaks into the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a definition by nickname rather than a synonym: it is what America's enemies, notably Iran's leaders since 1979, call it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Great Satan is the hostile nickname Ayatollah Khomeini gave the United States, so it can stand for America.

definitions.meaning: decimal counting is counting in tens, so this sense only appears once the answer is split in two

explanation.walkthrough: A decimal system is one of ten, so read the answer as two words and it describes "decimal" exactly.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: frequently, which is many times, and split as of ten, which is what decimal means.

clue.text: Side with cured meat or game

parts.note: the back is one side of a thing

explanation.surface: A menu offering a side dish with ham, or game birds instead.
explanation.walkthrough: "Game" looks like the meat on the menu, but it is a board game.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: backgammon is a board game of dice and counters for two players.

indicators.note: P is the abbreviation for power, and a machine powered down has had it switched off, so the P goes

parts.note: a partisan is a guerrilla fighter

explanation.surface: A rebel's boat has its engines cut and drifts.
explanation.walkthrough: "Craft" is an adjective here, as in craft beer or artisan bread: made by hand in small batches, not a boat.
explanation.definitionFit: An adjectival synonym: craft cheese and artisan cheese both mean handmade in small batches.

indicators.note: about means around, so the first piece goes round the outside of the next

explanation.surface: A news item on religious texts written about English citizens.
explanation.walkthrough: "About" wants to mean concerning, which suits a book; here it wraps one piece round another.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: nationals are citizens of a country, and people of Korea are one such group.

parts.note: the cooler is slang for prison, and prisons are divided into wings or sections

explanation.surface: Someone asking whether a quieter league division gets a cup.
explanation.walkthrough: "Cooler" sounds like colder or calmer, but it is slang for jail, and a ward is one section of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example, hence the question mark: a trophy is one kind of award, given for winning.

clue.text: Spirit of show can be amazing

parts.note: can is US slang for the buttocks, and showing them to someone has its own verb

explanation.surface: A review saying the spirit of a stage show can be amazing.
explanation.walkthrough: "Can" reads as a verb, but it pairs with "show" as a noun: showing your can is mooning.
explanation.definitionFit: A slang sense: moonshine is illicitly distilled spirit, especially US corn whiskey, named for being made by night.

definitions.meaning: not a lower-case letter but a short written message
A in music, one of the seven named pitches; the question mark flags an example

explanation.walkthrough: "A small letter" looks like it means a lower-case a, which the second "A" seems to confirm.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: a note is a brief letter, and A is one of the notes of the musical scale.

clue.text: Pet about to sit on head

indicators.note: in a down answer, a piece that sits on another is written above it

parts.note: noodle is slang for the head

explanation.surface: A pet about to plonk itself on your head, as cats do.
explanation.walkthrough: "Pet" is the verb, to kiss and cuddle, not an animal.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal synonym: to pet, in the old sense of kissing and cuddling, is to canoodle.

parts.note: not an admirer but a machine that moves air, the kind fitted in kitchens and bathrooms
the dentist's signature job is pulling teeth out

explanation.walkthrough: An extractor fan pulls air out of a room, and a dentist pulls teeth out, so the fan of the dentist is the one that extracts.
explanation.definitionFit: A pun on two senses: a kitchen extractor is a fan, and a tooth-pulling dentist is an extractor too.

parts.note: a spell of an illness, as in a coughing fit

explanation.surface: Someone worried that having a seizure is a concern.
explanation.walkthrough: "Concerning" looks like an adjective, worrying, which the surface uses; it is the preposition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as prepositions: a book concerning birds is a book about birds.

indicators.note: by means beside, so the next piece stands next to the first

parts.note: to tan someone's hide is to beat them

explanation.surface: A chart note: a pop hit by the band Journey.
explanation.walkthrough: Pop is fizzy drink, not music. Journey's capital letter makes it look like the rock band.
explanation.definitionFit: A brand name as example: Tango is a British fizzy orange soft drink, and fizzy drink is pop.

parts.note: slap is theatre slang for make-up

explanation.surface: A put-down of someone's careless way of doing their make-up.
explanation.walkthrough: "Make-up" looks like part of the picture of a messy face, but it is the old theatrical slang word for greasepaint.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: slapdash work is hasty and careless, which is sloppy.

clue.text: Siren goes off by small exits

indicators.note: something off has gone wrong or bad, so the letters are out of order
by means beside, so the next piece stands next to the anagram

explanation.surface: An alarm sounds beside the small fire exits.
explanation.walkthrough: "Goes off" reads as the alarm sounding; the anagram indicator is only "off", and "goes" is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal synonym: an egression is a going out, from the Latin for step out, so egressions are exits.

clue.text: A layer of ore close to desert

parts.note: a band is a seam or layer in rock
on can mean next to, as in a house on the river

explanation.surface: A prospector finds a seam of ore near the desert.
explanation.walkthrough: "Desert" looks like the sandy place, which suits the mining picture, but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as verbs: to desert a post or a person is to leave them behind for good.

indicators.note: letters moved around are shifted out of their order

explanation.surface: Some other boys hanging around town.
explanation.walkthrough: "Around town" reads as lads out on the streets; "around" is the instruction and "town" alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Aldershot is a garrison town in Hampshire, England, long home to the British Army.

explanation.surface: A boy getting seasick on a voyage.
explanation.walkthrough: "Sickening at sea" reads as seasickness, but the split is after "sickening".
explanation.definitionFit: A loose synonym, hence the question mark: a ship under way is out on the water, at sea.

definitions.meaning: as a verb: scents with burning spices, as in a church

explanation.surface: Scent imported from Angers, a city in France.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital letter dresses "Angers" up as the French city; it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses of one spelling: to perfume with incense (stress on the first syllable) and to enrage (stress on the second).

indicators.note: a mirror reflection shows things backwards
in an across answer, a piece on another is placed next to it

parts.note: to dress a horse or hair is to groom it

explanation.surface: A lawyer thinking over the bridegroom's wedding speech.
explanation.walkthrough: "Groom" is the verb, as in grooming a horse, not the man at the altar; "reflecting" looks like thinking it over.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal synonym: an address is a speech delivered to an audience, like an inaugural address.

indicators.note: a word with no head has lost its first letter
by means beside, so the next piece stands next to the first

parts.note: LAUNCH, to send off, loses its L

explanation.surface: A company baffled by a message without a heading.
explanation.walkthrough: "Firm" looks like a company, and "stumped" like baffled; one is an adjective and the other is cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a staunch ally is loyal and unwavering, firm in support.

parts.note: the Home Counties surround London, in the South East of England

explanation.surface: Hiding loot somewhere near London, or on a Greek island.
explanation.walkthrough: "In" looks like it wants a container, but it only joins the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A less common sense: besides discharging a fluid, to secrete means to hide away, to stash.

indicators.note: the first piece goes inside the next

explanation.surface: A sports squad out drinking until everything goes blurry.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface wants "drink" as the beer and "hazy" as the result; the drink is the verb sup, wrapped round the team.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrasal verb: glass that fogs with condensation becomes hazy.

clue.text: In bars, be up for port

indicators.note: up as in stirred up or messed up, so the letters are thrown out of order

explanation.surface: Advice in pubs: order the port.
explanation.walkthrough: "Port" invites the fortified wine, which suits the bar; it is a harbour city.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Brisbane, capital of Queensland in Australia, is a port on the Brisbane River.

clue.text: Bit of a character sacks turns

indicators.note: a word that turns faces the other way, so it is read backwards

parts.note: to sack someone is to fire them

explanation.surface: A bit of an eccentric sacks people on a whim.
explanation.walkthrough: "Character" looks like a person; it is a printed letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A typographic sense: a serif is the small finishing stroke on a printed letter, so it is part of a character.

definitions.meaning: as a verb: steals, takes for oneself
as a verb: arrests, as police collar a suspect

explanation.surface: Two parts of a shirt, pockets and collars.
explanation.walkthrough: Both look like nouns from the tailor's; both are verbs, stealing and arresting.
explanation.definitionFit: Two British slang senses: to nick is to steal, and police nick a suspect when they arrest them.

parts.note: a cat is jazz slang for a guy, a man
Companion of Honour, a British order

explanation.surface: A man and his partner might be the answer at 22 across.
explanation.walkthrough: The "22" is not a cross-reference to BRISBANE but the number in Joseph Heller's novel title Catch-22.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by allusion: Heller's no-win rule Catch-22 gave English its phrase, so this word could be followed by 22.

indicators.note: in a down answer, a piece put on another is placed on top of it

parts.note: a short form of Henry, as Shakespeare's Prince Hal
O in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A phone call: Henry rings, having put on the Oscars.
explanation.walkthrough: "Oscar" suggests the film award; it is only the letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a halo is the ring of light round a saint's head or round the moon.

parts.note: the char is a fish of the trout family

explanation.surface: A pickled fish.
explanation.walkthrough: The word may be new, so the wordplay does the work; the fish looks like part of the pickle but gives the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A loanword: achar is the Hindi and Urdu name for the spiced South Asian pickles served with curry.

clue.text: A couple on horse, say, for a second

parts.note: horse is slang for heroin, and people on it feel more numb

explanation.surface: Two people riding one horse, just for a moment.
explanation.walkthrough: NUMBER is not the counting word but numb-er, more numb; the couple on heroin are number.
explanation.definitionFit: A noun sense: a second is a deputy or assistant, the person ranked just below the leader.

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over, so its letters spill out of order

explanation.surface: A clumsy, flabby oaf knocks over the soup.
explanation.walkthrough: "Flabby" looks like a description of the oaf, but it stands apart as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: someone unfit and soft round the middle is flabby.

indicators.note: the answer is exactly half the letters of the next word, taken from its middle

parts.note: the middle four of its eight letters

explanation.surface: Someone only fitfully keen: so enthused, but only half the time.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket reads as a comment on the enthusiasm, but it is the instruction: take half of the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean therefore, or in this way.
